name: Cheek implants

lead: Cheek implants are solid synthetic shapes, usually silicone or porous polyethylene, placed through the mouth onto or under the cheekbone to make the midface more projected or fuller. They are used for flat cheekbones, asymmetry, ageing and facial feminisation, and are discussed on looksmaxxing forums as a way to get higher cheekbones.

Reviews of the surgical literature report high patient satisfaction and low complication rates, but the evidence is mostly retrospective series. Forum users debate malar versus submalar shapes and custom versus stock implants.

paras: An implant is positioned over the malar bone (malar), below it (submalar) or both, and fixed with sutures or screws, adding volume and projection that is permanent unless the implant is removed.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 3,701 patients found a 7.4% complication rate for malar implants (10.7% across facial implants), with heterogeneity. Reported issues include infection, displacement, visible prominence and asymmetry. Implants are Rx surgical devices placed by a surgeon under anesthesia.

lead: Cheek implants, also called malar or submalar implants, are solid alloplastic (synthetic) devices placed over or beneath the cheekbone to increase midface projection or fullness. They are used to correct congenital cheekbone underdevelopment, asymmetry and age-related volume loss, and in gender-affirming facial surgery, and they are discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a way to obtain higher or more angular cheekbones.[1][2][3]

The usual materials are silicone and porous high-density polyethylene (sold as Medpor), with expanded PTFE also used. The implant is typically inserted through an incision inside the mouth and stabilised with sutures or screws.[1][4][5] Reviews describe the result as permanent but reversible, since the implant can be removed.[1]

Published evidence consists mainly of reviews and case series rather than randomised trials. A 2025 meta-analysis of 48 studies reported an overall complication rate of 10.7% for facial skeletal implants and 7.4% for malar implants specifically, with substantial heterogeneity between studies.[6] A 2018 systematic review found that malar implants had a high incidence of prominence problems.[4] A 2008 review noted that enthusiasm for cheek implants appeared to be declining in favour of soft-tissue approaches such as fat and fillers.[7]
infobox: Removable, but porous materials may integrate with tissue

paras: Cheek implants are grouped by where they sit. Malar (shell) implants rest on the cheekbone and are intended to raise and sharpen the cheekbone contour. Submalar implants sit lower and fill a hollow or flat midface, producing a rounder cheek. Combined implants address both areas.[5][8]

Silicone and porous polyethylene are the two materials most often studied. Silicone is smooth and easier to remove; porous polyethylene allows tissue ingrowth, which can anchor it but may make later removal harder.[4][5] Custom implants designed from CT scans are also produced, and are discussed heavily in online communities.[9][10]

Surgeons describe malar augmentation for patients with flat cheekbones, midface hypoplasia, congenital asymmetry, or volume loss from ageing.[1] An early series reported using perforated silicone implants to make the face appear more oval and youthful, and to treat congenital or traumatic cheek deficiencies.[11]

Cheek augmentation is also a component of facial feminisation surgery, where high cheekbones and a full malar area are regarded as feminine features. The options in that setting are fillers, fat grafting and implants.[2][12]

Hyaluronic acid fillers and autologous fat are less invasive, adjustable and reversible, but require repeat treatment or have uncertain long-term retention.[2] Midface lifts and thread-based techniques are other soft-tissue options discussed in the literature.[7]

A 2022 review of recent literature concluded that overall patient satisfaction with alloplastic malar implants is high and complication rates are low, and that outcomes are likely comparable with other modalities in suitable hands.[3] A 1999 five-year retrospective review of a silicone midface implant and a one-year multicentre evaluation of preformed augmentation shapes (including malar implants) are among the older clinical series.[13][14]
Most evidence is retrospective, with variable follow-up, from 2 weeks to 15 years in one review.[4]

The 2018 systematic review of 626 polyethylene and 365 silicone cases found more infections and displacements with silicone, more prominence problems with polyethylene, and low exposure and extrusion rates for both. It noted that malar implants had a high incidence of prominence problems compared with chin and mandibular implants.[4]

The 2025 meta-analysis of 3,701 patients reported pooled complication rates of 10.7% for all facial skeletal implants, and 7.4% for malar implants, with high heterogeneity.[6] Reviews also list infection, migration and visibility as implant-related complications.[2]
An analysis of malpractice litigation related to facial implant surgery has also been published.[15]

Silicone malar implants were being used in the 1960s; a 1975 report described 52 cases since 1964.[11] Augmentation malarplasty was reported in the early 1980s,[16] and silicone and porous implants became standard materials in subsequent decades.[17][4] A 1997 French study examined coral blocks for cheek augmentation.[18]

Human data are limited to retrospective series, a small number of prospective evaluations and systematic reviews. A one-year prospective multicentre evaluation of preformed implants included 82 patients receiving nasal, chin and malar implants.[14] A prospective study of coral blocks in 23 patients was published in 1997.[18] No randomised trial comparing malar implants with other cheek augmentation methods appears among the sources reviewed here.[3][4][6]

On looksmax.org, cheek implants are discussed as a hardmaxxing option for people who consider their midface flat or recessed, sometimes as an alternative to a Le Fort III osteotomy.[8] Threads cover choosing surgeons, comparing off-the-shelf and custom designs, and combining implants with other procedures such as jaw and chin implants, brow lifts or fat grafts.[8][19][20][10] Some members travel abroad for multi-procedure packages, and one poster reported a cost of about US$15,000 for a package that included cheek implants.[19]

lore.intro: Cheek implants are discussed on looksmax.org as one of several midface hardmaxxing options, with debate over implant type, design and surgeon choice.[8][20]

claims.claim: Most cheek implants are the 'apple cheek' submalar type, which gives a bloated look, while malar implants give a defined, angular look.
Custom-designed implants are better than off-the-shelf implants.
Cheek implants can approximate the effect of a Le Fort III midface advancement.
Implants are a safe and permanent option when done by a skilled surgeon.

timeline.event: A surgical series begins using perforated silicone malar implants (reported 1975).[11]
Augmentation malarplasty is described in Archives of Otolaryngology.[16]
A five-year review of a silastic midfacial malar implant is published.[13]
A review notes declining enthusiasm for cheek implants relative to soft-tissue treatments.[7]
Systematic review compares polyethylene and silicone facial implants.[4]
Meta-analysis of 3,701 patients reports a 7.4% complication rate for malar implants.[6]
